content: Homeobox protein CDX-1 is a protein encoded by the CDX1 gene in humans. This protein is expressed during the development of the endoderm and continues to be expressed in the intestine throughout adulthood. Within the intestine, CDX1 protein expression is highest in the intestinal crypts and decreases progressively along the intestinal villi. The CDX1 gene belongs to the caudal-related homeobox transcription factor family. The protein it encodes functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that regulates gene expression specific to the intestine and plays a role in the differentiation of enterocytes. CDX1 has been shown to induce the expression of the intestinal alkaline phosphatase gene and inhibit the transcriptional activity of the beta-catenin/T-cell factor complex. In addition to its role in intestinal development, CDX1 is also implicated in embryonic epicardial development. Research has demonstrated that CDX proteins suppress cardiac differentiation in both zebrafish and mouse embryonic stem cells, although the precise mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear. CDX1 is transiently expressed in the embryonic heart at approximately 11.5 days post coitum (dpc). This transient expression is believed to promote the epicardial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), which is essential for proper cardiovascular development. Low-dose induction of CDX1 has been shown to enhance the migration and differentiation of epicardium-derived cells into vascular smooth muscle cells. In contrast, sustained high-dose induction of CDX1 or a deficiency in CDX1 impairs the ability of these cells to migrate and differentiate into smooth muscle, a process mediated by TGF-β1. Additionally, CDX1 induction has been found to alter the expression of genes involved in cell adhesion, EMT, and angiogenesis. Thus, beyond its established roles in intestinal patterning and differentiation, CDX1 is also critical for epicardial development and the proper formation of cardiovascular structures.
